title: Basic Mathematics for Physics
subtitle: Step-by-Step Visual & Conceptual Foundation: Algebra, Trigonometry, Coordinate Graphs, Calculus (Differentiation & Integration) & Vectors
introduction:
Why Do We Study Basic Mathematics First?

In Class 9 and 10, forces and speeds were mostly constant numbers, so simple arithmetic ($s = v \times t$) was enough.

In Class 11, Class 12, and JEE Advanced, physical quantities change continuously every microsecond. To read and solve Physics effortlessly, you need 6 mathematical tools:

  • 1. Algebra & Binomial Approximation: To simplify complex power formulas when one distance is much smaller than another ($h \ll R$).
  • 2. Trigonometry & Phasors: To split tilted forces into components and combine oscillating waves in SHM, AC, and Optics.
  • 3. Coordinate Geometry & Graphs: Because JEE questions hide velocity, acceleration, and work inside the Slope and Area of curves.
  • 4. Differentiation ($dy/dx$): A mathematical microscope that finds the exact rate of change at a single instant of time.
  • 5. Integration ($\int y\,dx$): A mathematical accumulator that adds up infinitely many tiny variable pieces (like work done by a spring).
  • 6. Vectors: The algebra of arrows, where direction matters just as much as magnitude.

topics.title: Algebraic Tools: Quadratic Equations, Binomial Approximation, AP/GP & Logarithms
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Quadratic Equations in Physics
Definition: Quadratic Equation

Any equation where the highest power of the unknown variable $x$ (such as time $t$ or position $x$) is $2$:

$$ax^2 + bx + c = 0 \qquad (a \neq 0)$$
Standard Quadratic Form where $a, b, c$ are known physical constants

Its two solutions (called roots $x_1$ and $x_2$) are given by the Quadratic Formula:

$$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$
Here $D = b^2 - 4ac$ is called the Discriminant

Physical Meaning of the Discriminant ($D = b^2 - 4ac$):

  • Case 1 ($D > 0$): Two distinct real roots. Example: A ball thrown upward crosses a height $h$ twice—once going up ($t_1$) and once coming down ($t_2$).
  • Case 2 ($D = 0$): One repeated real root ($x = -b/2a$). Example: The ball just touches its maximum height $H_{\max}$ at a single instant.
  • Case 3 ($D < 0$): No real root. Physical meaning: The event is impossible (the ball never reaches that height!).
Root RelationFormulaWhere You Use It in JEE Physics
Sum of Roots$$x_1 + x_2 = -\frac{b}{a}$$In vertical motion $\frac{1}{2}gt^2 - ut + h = 0$, sum of times is $t_1 + t_2 = \frac{2u}{g} = T_{\text{flight}}$.
Product of Roots$$x_1 x_2 = \frac{c}{a}$$In vertical motion, product of times is $t_1 t_2 = \frac{2h}{g} \implies h = \frac{1}{2}g t_1 t_2$.
Difference of Roots$$|x_1 - x_2| = \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{|a|}$$Finds the time duration $\Delta t = |t_2 - t_1|$ spent by a projectile above height $h$.
1.2 The Binomial Theorem & Physics Approximation

First-Time Reader Intuition:

Suppose $x$ is a very tiny number compared to $1$, such as $x = 0.001$.

Then $x^2 = 0.000001$ (one in a million) and $x^3 = 0.000000001$ (one in a billion)!

Because higher powers of a tiny fraction become vanishingly small, we can drop $x^2, x^3, \dots$ whenever $|x| \ll 1$.

$$(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2 + \dots$$
Exact Newton Binomial Expansion (valid for any real exponent $n$)
$$(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx \qquad \text{and} \qquad (1 - x)^n \approx 1 - nx$$
Physics Binomial Approximation — Valid STRICTLY when $|x| \ll 1$ (typically $|x| \le 0.05$)
1.3 Geometric Progression (GP) & Infinite Sum
Definition: Geometric Progression (GP)

A sequence where each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a constant ratio $r$: $a,\; ar,\; ar^2,\; ar^3, \dots$

$$S_n = \frac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r} \qquad \text{and for } |r| < 1: \qquad S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 - r}$$
$a =$ First Term, $r =$ Common Ratio ($S_\infty$ is used in infinite bouncing balls & infinite charge grids)
1.4 Exponential ($e^x$) & Natural Logarithm ($\ln x$) Identities
  • Product Rule: $\ln(A \cdot B) = \ln A + \ln B$
  • Quotient Rule: $\ln\left(\frac{A}{B}\right) = \ln A - \ln B$
  • Power Rule: $\ln(A^k) = k \ln A$
  • Base Values & Base-10 Conversion: $\ln(e) = 1, \quad \ln(1) = 0, \quad \ln(x) = 2.303 \log_{10}(x)$
Worked Concept Example:
Find the approximate value of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1.02}}$ without a calculator.
Solution:
Write $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1.02}} = (1 + 0.02)^{-1/2}$.
Here $x = 0.02 \ll 1$ and $n = -\frac{1}{2}$.
Using $(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx$:
$$(1 + 0.02)^{-1/2} \approx 1 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)(0.02) = 1 - 0.01 = 0.99$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation 1 • Step 1

Completing the Square for $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$:

Divide the entire equation by $a$ and move the constant term to the right side:

$$x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x = -\frac{c}{a}$$
Derivation 1 • Step 2

Add $\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2$ to both sides so the left side becomes a perfect square:

$$\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2}{4a^2} - \frac{c}{a} = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$$
Derivation 1 • Step 3

Take the square root on both sides and isolate $x$:

$$x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm\frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$
Derivation 2 • Gravity at Small Altitude

How Binomial Approximation Derives $g' \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$:

Exact gravity at height $h$ above Earth of radius $R$ is:

$$g' = \frac{GM}{(R + h)^2}$$

Pull out $R^2$ from the denominator so the bracket starts with $1$:

$$g' = \frac{GM}{R^2\left(1 + \frac{h}{R}\right)^2} = g\left(1 + \frac{h}{R}\right)^{-2}$$

When $h \ll R$, let $x = \frac{h}{R} \ll 1$ and $n = -2$. Apply $(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx$:

$$g' \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Using Binomial Approximation When $x$ Is NOT Small):
    Students often use $g' = g(1 - 2h/R)$ at $h = R/2$, which gives $g' = 0$ (impossible!).
    How to Avoid: Since $h/R = 0.5$ is NOT $\ll 1$, you MUST use the exact formula $g' = \frac{g}{(1 + h/R)^2} = \frac{4}{9}g$. Only use $(1+x)^n \approx 1+nx$ when $|x| \le 0.05$.
  • Trap 2 (Forgetting to Factor Out the Larger Term First):
    In $(a + b)^n$ with $b \ll a$, always factor out $a^n$ first so the first term inside the bracket is $1$: $(a + b)^n = a^n(1 + b/a)^n \approx a^n\left(1 + n\frac{b}{a}\right)$.

topics.title: Trigonometry for Physics: Radian Measure, ASTC Rule, Identities, Small-Angle Approximation & Phasors
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Radian Measure vs. Degree Measure
Definition: One Radian (1 rad)

The plane angle subtended at the center of a circle by an arc whose length $s$ is equal to the radius $R$ of the circle.

$$\theta \text{ (in radians)} = \frac{\text{Arc Length }(s)}{\text{Radius }(R)} \implies s = R\theta$$
Conversion: $\pi\text{ rad} = 180^\circ \implies 1\text{ rad} = \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} \approx 57.3^\circ$
2.2 The 3–4–5 Physics Triangle ($37^\circ$ & $53^\circ$) & Standard Angles

A right triangle with sides $3, 4, 5$ has acute angles $37^\circ$ (opposite side $3$) and $53^\circ$ (opposite side $4$). Memorize this table for instant force resolution:

Ratio$0^\circ$$30^\circ (\pi/6)$$37^\circ$$45^\circ (\pi/4)$$53^\circ$$60^\circ (\pi/3)$$90^\circ (\pi/2)$$120^\circ$$180^\circ (\pi)$
$\sin\theta$$0$$\frac{1}{2}$$\frac{3}{5} = 0.6$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$\frac{4}{5} = 0.8$$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$1$$+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$0$
$\cos\theta$$1$$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$\frac{4}{5} = 0.8$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$\frac{3}{5} = 0.6$$\frac{1}{2}$$0$$-\frac{1}{2}$$-1$
$\tan\theta$$0$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$\frac{3}{4} = 0.75$$1$$\frac{4}{3} \approx 1.33$$\sqrt{3}$$\infty$$-\sqrt{3}$$0$
2.3 ASTC Quadrant Rule & Allied Angle Reduction

2-Step Rule for Any Large Angle like $(180^\circ - \theta)$ or $(90^\circ + \theta)$:

  1. Check Sign by Quadrant (ASTC):
    • Quadrant I ($0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$): All positive.
    • Quadrant II ($90^\circ$ to $180^\circ$): Sine ($\sin, \csc$) positive.
    • Quadrant III ($180^\circ$ to $270^\circ$): Tan ($\tan, \cot$) positive.
    • Quadrant IV ($270^\circ$ to $360^\circ$): Cos ($\cos, \sec$) positive.
  2. Check Function Change:
    • Multiples of $180^\circ$ ($180^\circ \pm \theta, 360^\circ \pm \theta$): Function stays the same.
    • Odd multiples of $90^\circ$ ($90^\circ \pm \theta, 270^\circ \pm \theta$): Function switches to co-function ($\sin \leftrightarrow \cos$, $\tan \leftrightarrow \cot$).
2.4 Essential Compound, Double-Angle & Degree-Reduction Identities
$$\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A\cos B \pm \cos A\sin B$$
$$\cos(A \pm B) = \cos A\cos B \mp \sin A\sin B$$
Compound Angle Addition & Subtraction Formulas
$$\sin(2\theta) = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \qquad \text{and} \qquad \cos(2\theta) = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta$$
Double-Angle Identities (Used in Projectile Range & Optics)
$$\sin^2\theta = \frac{1 - \cos(2\theta)}{2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \cos^2\theta = \frac{1 + \cos(2\theta)}{2}$$
Power-Reduction Identities (Mandatory for integrating $\sin^2\theta$ and $\cos^2\theta$ in AC & Waves)
2.5 Small-Angle Approximation (For Pendulums, Lenses & Interference)
$$\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta \approx \theta \text{ (in radians)} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \cos\theta \approx 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2} \approx 1$$
Valid when $\theta$ is very small ($\theta \le 5^\circ \approx 0.087\text{ rad}$)
Worked Concept Example:
A simple pendulum of length $L = 1\text{ m}$ is displaced by a tiny angle $\theta = 3^\circ$. Find the horizontal displacement $x = L\sin\theta$.
Solution:
First convert $\theta = 3^\circ$ to radians: $\theta = 3 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{\pi}{60}\text{ rad}$.
Using $\sin\theta \approx \theta$: $x \approx (1\text{ m}) \times \frac{\pi}{60} \approx 0.0523\text{ m} = 5.23\text{ cm}$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation • Step 1

Combining $y = a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$ into a Single Sine Wave (Phasor Resultant):

Multiply and divide the expression by $R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$:

$$y = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}\sin\theta + \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}\cos\theta\right)$$
Derivation • Step 2

Define phase angle $\alpha$ from a right triangle with base $a$, height $b$, and hypotenuse $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ so that $\cos\alpha = \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$ and $\sin\alpha = \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$ (meaning $\tan\alpha = \frac{b}{a}$):

$$y = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}(\sin\theta\cos\alpha + \cos\theta\sin\alpha) = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\sin(\theta + \alpha)$$
Derivation • Step 3

Since $\sin(\theta + \alpha)$ oscillates between $-1$ and $+1$, the extreme values of $y$ are:

$$y_{\max} = +\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad y_{\min} = -\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Putting Degrees into $\sin\theta \approx \theta$):
    Never write $\sin(2^\circ) \approx 2$! You MUST convert degrees into radians first: $\sin(2^\circ) \approx 2 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{\pi}{90}$.
  • Trap 2 (When $1 - \cos\theta$ Appears):
    In pendulum height $h = L(1 - \cos\theta)$, setting $\cos\theta \approx 1$ gives $h = 0$! Whenever $1 - \cos\theta$ is subtracted, use the second-order identity $1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2) \approx \frac{\theta^2}{2}$, so $h \approx \frac{1}{2}L\theta^2$.

topics.title: Coordinate Geometry & Reading Physics Graphs (Straight Line, Parabola, Hyperbola, Ellipse & Exponential)
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 The 4-Step Protocol for Reading Any Physics Graph

Whenever a JEE problem gives you a graph between vertical variable $y$ and horizontal variable $x$, check these 4 things in order:

  1. Check the Exact Axes & Units: Is it $v$ vs $t$, or $v$ vs $x$, or $v^2$ vs $x$?
  2. Check the Intercepts: Where the graph cuts the $y$-axis gives the value at $x = 0$. Where it cuts the $x$-axis gives the root where $y = 0$.
  3. Check the Tangent Slope ($m = \tan\theta = \frac{dy}{dx}$): Represents the instantaneous rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$.
  4. Check the Area Under the Curve ($\text{Area} = \int y\,dx$): Represents the accumulated product of $y$ and $dx$.
3.2 Straight Line Equations ($y = mx + c$)
$$m = \tan\theta = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \qquad \text{and} \qquad y = mx + c$$
$m =$ Slope of the line, $c =$ y-intercept (value of $y$ where $x = 0$)
3.3 Master Atlas of the 6 Curves Used Across Physics
Curve TypeStandard EquationHow to Recognize ShapeDirect Physics Examples
1. Straight Line$y = mx + c$Constant slope $m$.$v = u + at$; Photoelectric $K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi_0$.
2. Parabola$y = ax^2 + bx + c$Symmetric U-curve. Opens Upward (Cup) if $a > 0$; opens Downward (Cap) if $a < 0$.Projectile path $y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$; Spring Energy $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$.
3. Rectangular Hyperbola$x \cdot y = \text{constant}$
or $y \propto \frac{1}{x^n}$		Approaches both axes asymptotically without touching them. Larger $n$ gives a steeper drop.Isothermal gas law $PV = \text{const}$; Gravitation/Coulomb $F \propto 1/r^2$.
4. Circle & Ellipse$\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$Closed oval loop with semi-axes $a$ and $b$ (Circle if $a = b = R$).SHM velocity-position graph $\frac{v^2}{(\omega A)^2} + \frac{x^2}{A^2} = 1$; Planetary orbits.
5. Exponential Decay$y = y_0 e^{-\lambda x}$Starts at $y_0$ at $x=0$, drops to $0.37y_0$ at $x = 1/\lambda$, approaches $0$ as $x \to \infty$.Radioactive decay $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$; Capacitor discharging.
6. Exponential Saturation$y = y_0(1 - e^{-x/\tau})$Starts at $0$, reaches $0.63y_0$ at $x = \tau$, levels off at horizontal asymptote $y_0$.Capacitor charging $q = CV(1 - e^{-t/RC})$; Raindrop terminal velocity.
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation • Linearization of Curves

How to Turn a Curved Physics Formula into a Straight-Line Graph:

Consider a particle accelerating from initial speed $u$ with constant acceleration $a$:

$$v^2 = u^2 + 2ax$$

1. If you plot $v$ on the y-axis against $x$ on the x-axis, the graph is a parabola ($v = \sqrt{u^2 + 2ax}$).

2. If you instead plot $Y = v^2$ on the y-axis against $X = x$ on the x-axis, the equation becomes:

$$Y = (2a)X + u^2 \qquad \text{which matches } Y = mX + c$$

Therefore, the $v^2$ vs $x$ graph is a straight line whose y-intercept is $c = u^2$ and whose slope is $m = 2a \implies a = \frac{\text{Slope}}{2}$!

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Confusing Chord Slope $y/x$ with Tangent Slope $dy/dx$):
    On a curved $x$-$t$ graph, $\frac{x}{t}$ is the slope of the secant line from the origin (average velocity), whereas $\frac{dx}{dt}$ is the slope of the tangent line at that instant (instantaneous velocity).
  • Trap 2 (Using Visual Angle $\tan\theta$ When Axis Scales Differ):
    If the y-axis is marked in steps of $50\text{ m/s}$ and the x-axis in steps of $2\text{ s}$, never use a protractor angle $\tan\theta$! Always compute $\frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ directly from the axis numbers.
  • Trap 3 (Reading Slope of $v$ vs $x$ Graph as Acceleration):
    On a $v$-$x$ graph, slope is $\frac{dv}{dx}$, NOT acceleration! True acceleration is $a = v\frac{dv}{dx} = (\text{y-coordinate}) \times (\text{slope})$.

topics.title: Limits & Differential Calculus from First Principles (Secant-to-Tangent, Standard Derivatives, Chain, Product & Quotient Rules)
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Is a Derivative?

Imagine driving $200\text{ km}$ in $4\text{ hours}$. Your Average Speed is $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{200}{4} = 50\text{ km/h}$.

But your car's speedometer shows your speed right now at a single instant! How do we calculate speed over a time interval that shrinks to zero ($\Delta t \to 0$)?

We take a tiny time window $\Delta t$ and find the limiting value of the ratio $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ as $\Delta t$ approaches zero. Geometrically, the Secant Line across two points merges into the Tangent Line at a single point!

Definition: Derivative from First Principles

The instantaneous rate of change of $y = f(x)$ with respect to $x$ equals the limit of the secant slope $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ as $\Delta x \to 0$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = f'(x) = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} = \tan\theta_{\text{tangent}}$$
Read $\frac{dy}{dx}$ as “Derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$” (NOT $d$ times $y$ divided by $d$ times $x$!)
4.2 Master Table of Standard Derivatives
Function $y = f(x)$Derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$Quick Physics Example
Constant $c$$$0$$If position $x = 5\text{ m}$ (stationary), velocity $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 0$.
Power Rule $x^n$$$n x^{n-1}$$$\frac{d}{dx}(x^3) = 3x^2$; $\quad \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = -\frac{1}{x^2}$; $\quad \frac{d}{dx}(\sqrt{x}) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$.
$\sin x$$$+\cos x$$If $x = A\sin(\omega t)$, then $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = +A\omega\cos(\omega t)$.
$\cos x$$$-\sin x$$Notice the minus sign! $\frac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = -\sin x$.
$\tan x$$$\sec^2 x$$$\frac{d}{dx}(\cot x) = -\csc^2 x$; $\quad \frac{d}{dx}(\sec x) = \sec x\tan x$.
Exponential $e^x$$$e^x$$For $y = e^{kx}$, derivative is $\frac{dy}{dx} = k e^{kx}$.
Natural Log $\ln x$$$\frac{1}{x}$$For $\log_a x$, derivative is $\frac{1}{x\ln a}$.
4.3 The 4 Operational Rules of Differentiation
Rule 1 • Sum & Constant Multiple
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[c_1 u(x) \pm c_2 v(x)\right] = c_1 \frac{du}{dx} \pm c_2 \frac{dv}{dx}$$
Rule 2 • Product Rule (UV Rule)

When two functions of $x$ are multiplied together:

$$\frac{d}{dx}(u \cdot v) = u\frac{dv}{dx} + v\frac{du}{dx}$$
(First $\times$ Derivative of Second) $+$ (Second $\times$ Derivative of First)
Rule 3 • Quotient Rule (U/V Rule)

When one function of $x$ is divided by another:

$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{u}{v}\right) = \frac{v\frac{du}{dx} - u\frac{dv}{dx}}{v^2}$$
(Bottom $\times$ Derivative of Top $-$ Top $\times$ Derivative of Bottom) $\div$ (Bottom)$^2$
Rule 4 • The Chain Rule (Outside-Inside Rule)

When a function is nested inside another function, $y = f(g(x))$, differentiate the outer function first (keeping the inside untouched), then multiply by the derivative of the inner function:

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx} = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$$
Worked Concept Example:
Differentiate $y = \sin(3t^2 + 5)$ with respect to $t$.
Solution:
1. Outer function is $\sin(u)$, whose derivative is $\cos(u) = \cos(3t^2 + 5)$.
2. Inner function is $u = 3t^2 + 5$, whose derivative with respect to $t$ is $\frac{du}{dt} = 6t$.
3. Multiply them together by the Chain Rule:
$$\frac{dy}{dt} = 6t \cos(3t^2 + 5)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof 1 • Power Rule from First Principles

Let $f(x) = x^n$. Substitute into the limit definition:

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{(x + \Delta x)^n - x^n}{\Delta x} = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{x^n\left(1 + \frac{\Delta x}{x}\right)^n - x^n}{\Delta x}$$

Since $\Delta x \to 0$, we have $\frac{\Delta x}{x} \ll 1$. Apply the Binomial Approximation $\left(1 + \frac{\Delta x}{x}\right)^n \approx 1 + n\frac{\Delta x}{x}$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{x^n + n x^{n-1}\Delta x - x^n}{\Delta x} = n x^{n-1}$$
Proof 2 • The Kinematics Chain-Rule Identity

How $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$ Becomes $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ When Velocity Depends on Position $x$:

By the Chain Rule, multiply and divide $\frac{dv}{dt}$ by $dx$:

$$a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{dx} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt}$$

Since $\frac{dx}{dt} = v$, this immediately gives the famous JEE identity:

$$a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Plugging in Numbers BEFORE Differentiating):
    To find velocity at $t = 2\text{ s}$ for $x(t) = 5t^2$, NEVER substitute $t = 2$ first (because $x(2) = 20$ and $\frac{d}{dt}(20) = 0$!). Always differentiate symbolically first ($v = 10t$) and substitute $t = 2\text{ s}$ at the very end ($v = 20\text{ m/s}$).
  • Trap 2 (Forgetting $\frac{dr}{dt}$ in Related Rates):
    When differentiating sphere volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ with respect to time $t$, don't stop at $4\pi r^2$—multiply by $\frac{dr}{dt}$ via the Chain Rule: $\frac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2 \frac{dr}{dt}$.

topics.title: Applications of Derivatives: Physical Rate Dictionary & Maxima-Minima Optimization
topics.theoryHtml:
5.1 Where Derivatives Appear Across Physics
Physical QuantityFirst DerivativeSecond Derivative
Position $x(t)$Velocity $v = \frac{dx}{dt}$Acceleration $a = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = \frac{dv}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}$
Angle $\theta(t)$Angular Velocity $\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt}$Angular Acceleration $\alpha = \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = \omega\frac{d\omega}{d\theta}$
Charge $q(t)$Electric Current $I = \frac{dq}{dt}$Rate of current change $\frac{dI}{dt}$ (Inductor EMF $= -L\frac{dI}{dt}$)
Potential Energy $U(x)$Conservative Force $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$Stability & Spring Constant $k = +\frac{d^2U}{dx^2}$
5.2 Maxima & Minima (Finding Peak Values & Equilibrium)

Visual Intuition (Hilltop vs. Valley Bottom):

• At the exact top of a hill (Local Maximum), the tangent line is horizontal ($\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$), and the curve bends downward (concave down, so slope is decreasing: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} < 0$).

• At the exact bottom of a valley (Local Minimum), the tangent line is also horizontal ($\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$), and the curve bends upward (concave up, so slope is increasing: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} > 0$).

$$\text{For Maximum at } x = x_0: \qquad \frac{dy}{dx}\Big|_{x_0} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\Big|_{x_0} < 0$$
$$\text{For Minimum at } x = x_0: \qquad \frac{dy}{dx}\Big|_{x_0} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\Big|_{x_0} > 0$$
Worked Concept Example:
The height of a stone is $y(t) = 40t - 5t^2$ meters. Find the maximum height using calculus.
Solution:
1. Set first derivative to zero: $\frac{dy}{dt} = 40 - 10t = 0 \implies t = 4\text{ s}$.
2. Check second derivative: $\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} = -10 < 0$ (confirms a maximum!).
3. Substitute $t = 4\text{ s}$ into $y(t)$: $y_{\max} = 40(4) - 5(4)^2 = 160 - 80 = 80\text{ m}$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation • Maximum Power Transfer Theorem

Find the external load resistance $R$ that draws maximum power from a battery of EMF $E$ and internal resistance $r$:

Current in the circuit is $I = \frac{E}{R + r}$, so thermal power in resistor $R$ is:

$$P(R) = I^2 R = \frac{E^2 R}{(R + r)^2}$$
Step 2 • Differentiate with Respect to $R$

Apply the Quotient Rule to $\frac{R}{(R+r)^2}$ and set $\frac{dP}{dR} = 0$:

$$\frac{dP}{dR} = E^2 \left[ \frac{(R + r)^2(1) - R \cdot 2(R + r)}{(R + r)^4} \right] = E^2 \left[ \frac{r - R}{(R + r)^3} \right] = 0$$
Step 3 • Solve for Optimal Load & Max Power
$$r - R = 0 \implies R = r \qquad \text{and} \qquad P_{\max} = \frac{E^2}{4r}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Stable vs. Unstable Equilibrium on Potential Energy $U(x)$ Graphs):
    Equilibrium ($F = -\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$) occurs wherever the slope of $U(x)$ is zero. A Minimum of $U(x)$ (valley bottom, $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} > 0$) is Stable Equilibrium, whereas a Maximum of $U(x)$ (hilltop, $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} < 0$) is Unstable Equilibrium!

topics.title: Integral Calculus: Indefinite & Definite Integrals, Signed Area Under Curves & Physics Differential Equations
topics.theoryHtml:
6.1 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Is Integration?

Differentiation slices a quantity into tiny pieces ($dy/dx$). Integration does the exact opposite: it glues infinitely many microscopic slices ($y\,dx$) together to find the total accumulated amount!

Geometrically, the definite integral $\int_a^b y(x)\,dx$ equals the Signed Area under the curve $y(x)$ between $x = a$ and $x = b$.

$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \Big[ F(x) \Big]_a^b = F(b) - F(a) \qquad \text{where } \frac{d}{dx}[F(x)] = f(x)$$
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: Upper Limit Value minus Lower Limit Value
6.2 Master Table of Standard Integrals
Integrand $f(x)$Indefinite Integral $\int f(x)\,dx$Key Rule / Physics Usage
$\int x^n\,dx \quad (n \neq -1)$$$\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$$Increase power by $1$, divide by the new power.
$\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \int x^{-1}\,dx$$$\ln|x| + C$$Used in Isothermal Work $W = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$.
$\int \sin(kx)\,dx$$$-\frac{\cos(kx)}{k} + C$$Divide by inner coefficient $k$!
$\int \cos(kx)\,dx$$$+\frac{\sin(kx)}{k} + C$$Used in Alternating Current & SHM impulse.
$\int e^{kx}\,dx$$$\frac{e^{kx}}{k} + C$$Used in RC circuits & radioactive decay laws.
6.3 Continuous Average Value of Any Function $\langle y \rangle$
$$\langle y \rangle_{[x_1, x_2]} = \frac{\int_{x_1}^{x_2} y(x)\,dx}{x_2 - x_1} = \frac{\text{Area under } y(x)}{\text{Base Width}}$$
Example: Average of $\sin^2(\omega t)$ or $\cos^2(\omega t)$ over a full cycle is $\frac{1}{2}$
Worked Concept Example:
A variable spring-like force $F(x) = (6x^2 + 4x)\text{ N}$ pushes a block from $x = 0$ to $x = 2\text{ m}$. Find the total work done.
Solution:
$$W = \int_0^2 (6x^2 + 4x)\,dx = \Big[ 2x^3 + 2x^2 \Big]_0^2 = \left(2(8) + 2(4)\right) - 0 = 24\text{ J}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation • Solving Physics Differential Equations by Separation of Variables

Case 1: When Acceleration Is a Function of Position $a(x)$:

Write $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$, separate $v\,dv$ on the left and $a(x)\,dx$ on the right, and integrate with matching limits:

$$v\frac{dv}{dx} = a(x) \implies \int_u^v v\,dv = \int_{x_0}^x a(x)\,dx \implies \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2} = \int_{x_0}^x a(x)\,dx$$
Case 2 • When Retardation Is Proportional to Speed ($a = -kv$)

Write $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = -kv$, bring $v$ under $dv$, and move $dt$ to the right:

$$\int_{v_0}^v \frac{dv}{v} = -k \int_0^t dt \implies \ln\left(\frac{v}{v_0}\right) = -kt \implies v(t) = v_0 e^{-kt}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Displacement vs. Distance in Definite Integrals):
    $\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v(t)\,dt$ subtracts area below the time axis ($A_1 - A_2$), giving Displacement. To find Distance, split the integral where $v(t) = 0$ and add absolute areas ($|A_1| + |A_2|$).
  • Trap 2 (Never Forget $\cos(0) = 1$ and $e^0 = 1$ at the Lower Limit!):
    When evaluating $[-\cos x]_0^\pi$ or $[e^{-x}]_0^t$, the lower limit $x = 0$ evaluates to $1$, NOT $0$!

topics.title: Scalars & Vectors: Parallelogram Law, 3D Unit Vectors, Dot Product & Cross Product
topics.theoryHtml:
7.1 What Makes a Quantity a True Vector?
Definition: Vector Quantity

A physical quantity that has magnitude, direction, AND obeys the Parallelogram Law of Vector Addition.

Note: Electric current $I$ has magnitude and direction, but adds by simple scalar arithmetic ($3\text{ A} + 4\text{ A} = 7\text{ A}$), so current is a Scalar!

7.2 Parallelogram Law of Vector Addition & Subtraction

When two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are placed Tail-to-Tail with angle $\theta$ between them:

$$R = |\vec{A} + \vec{B}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}$$
Magnitude of Resultant $\vec{R}$ and its angle $\alpha$ with $\vec{A}$
$$|\vec{A} - \vec{B}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 - 2AB\cos\theta}$$
Magnitude of Vector Subtraction ($\vec{A} - \vec{B}$)
$$\text{If } |\vec{A}| = |\vec{B}| = F: \qquad |\vec{A} + \vec{B}| = 2F\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \quad \text{and} \quad |\vec{A} - \vec{B}| = 2F\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)$$
High-Speed Equal-Vector Shortcut (Used heavily in Electrostatics, Circular Motion & Waves)
7.3 3D Orthogonal Unit Vectors ($\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$) & Direction Cosines
$$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k} \implies |\vec{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \hat{A} = \frac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$$
Direction Cosines $\cos\alpha = \frac{A_x}{A},\; \cos\beta = \frac{A_y}{A},\; \cos\gamma = \frac{A_z}{A}$ satisfy $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$
7.4 Scalar (Dot) Product vs. Vector (Cross) Product
PropertyScalar (Dot) Product $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}$Vector (Cross) Product $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$
Formula$$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$$ (Scalar output)$$\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = (AB\sin\theta)\,\hat{n}$$ (Vector $\perp$ to plane of $\vec{A}, \vec{B}$)
In Components$$A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z$$$$\hat{i}(A_y B_z - A_z B_y) - \hat{j}(A_x B_z - A_z B_x) + \hat{k}(A_x B_y - A_y B_x)$$
Zero ConditionPerpendicular Test: $\vec{A} \perp \vec{B} \iff \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$Parallel Test: $\vec{A} \parallel \vec{B} \iff \vec{A}\times\vec{B} = \vec{0}$
GeometryProjection of $\vec{A}$ on $\vec{B}$ is $A\cos\theta = \vec{A}\cdot\hat{B}$.$|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}| =$ Area of Parallelogram with sides $\vec{A}, \vec{B}$.
Physics Laws$W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}$, $\quad P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$, $\quad \Phi = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{A}$$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$, $\quad \vec{L} = \vec{r}\times\vec{p}$, $\quad \vec{F}_B = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation 1 • Parallelogram Law Proof

Drop a perpendicular from the head of $\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$ onto the line of $\vec{A}$:

• Total horizontal base $= A + B\cos\theta$

• Vertical height $= B\sin\theta$

By Pythagoras' theorem:

$$R^2 = (A + B\cos\theta)^2 + (B\sin\theta)^2 = A^2 + B^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) + 2AB\cos\theta = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta$$
Derivation 2 • Resolving Vector $\vec{A}$ Parallel & Perpendicular to $\vec{B}$

Scalar length of $\vec{A}$ along $\vec{B}$ is $\vec{A}\cdot\hat{B}$. Multiply by direction $\hat{B}$ to get the parallel vector component:

$$\vec{A}_{\parallel} = (\vec{A}\cdot\hat{B})\hat{B} = \left(\frac{\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}}{|\vec{B}|^2}\right)\vec{B} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \vec{A}_{\perp} = \vec{A} - \vec{A}_{\parallel}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Tail-to-Tail Angle Rule):
    Always slide two vectors so their tails touch before reading the angle $\theta$. If they touch head-to-tail with interior angle $\phi$, the true angle between the vectors is $\theta = 180^\circ - \phi$!
  • Trap 2 (Change in Velocity $|\Delta\vec{v}|$ vs. Change in Speed $\Delta v$):
    In uniform circular motion at speed $v$, speed change is $\Delta v = 0$, but the magnitude of the velocity vector change after turning by angle $\theta$ is $|\Delta\vec{v}| = 2v\sin(\theta/2)$.

conclusion:
Chapter Conclusion:

You now have the complete mathematical engine of Physics. Whenever a quantity changes at an instant, take its Derivative ($dy/dx$); whenever variable contributions accumulate over distance or time, take the Definite Integral ($\int y\,dx$); and whenever direction is involved, resolve vectors along orthogonal axes ($\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$).
summary:
• Binomial Approximation: $(1+x)^n \approx 1 + nx$ valid strictly when $|x| \ll 1$.
  • Harmonic Extremes: $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$ has maximum $+\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and minimum $-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
  • Calculus Duality: Tangent Slope $= \frac{dy}{dx}$; Signed Area Under Curve $= \int_a^b y\,dx$; Acceleration $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}$.
  • Optimization: At maximum or minimum, $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ (Maximum if $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} < 0$; Minimum if $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} > 0$).
  • Vectors: $|\vec{A} \pm \vec{B}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 \pm 2AB\cos\theta}$; $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0 \iff \vec{A} \perp \vec{B}$; $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = \vec{0} \iff \vec{A} \parallel \vec{B}$.

questions.prompt: Using the Binomial Approximation, find the value of $(1.004)^5 - (0.998)^{10}$ accurate to three decimal places.
A particle moves along the x-axis such that $x(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t + 6$ meters. At what instants of time $t$ is its velocity zero?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Differentiate position $x(t)$ with respect to $t$:

$$v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 6t^2 - 18t + 12 = 6(t - 1)(t - 2)$$

Step 2: Setting $v(t) = 0$ gives $t = 1\text{ s}$ and $t = 2\text{ s}$.

questions.prompt: If a force $\vec{F} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\text{ N}$ produces a displacement $\vec{s} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + c\hat{k}\text{ m}$ and performs zero work ($W = 0$), find $c$.
Evaluate the definite integral representing the impulse of an oscillating force: $J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 10\sin(2t)\,dt\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$.
Find the unit vector in the direction of $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$.

A particle moves in a circle of radius $2\text{ m}$ at constant speed $v = 10\text{ m/s}$. When it completes a quarter-circle ($\theta = 90^\circ$), what is the magnitude of the change in its velocity vector $|\Delta\vec{v}|$?
Find the value of $\sin(127^\circ) + \cos(143^\circ)$ using the 3-4-5 right triangle.
If $|\vec{A} + \vec{B}| = |\vec{A} - \vec{B}|$ for two non-zero vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, then the angle $\theta$ between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is:
Two forces of equal magnitude $F$ have a resultant whose magnitude is also equal to $F$. What is the angle between the two forces?
The potential energy of a diatomic molecule is $U(r) = \frac{A}{r^{12}} - \frac{B}{r^6}$. Find the equilibrium separation $r_0$ where $F(r) = 0$.

A particle's velocity varies with position $x$ as $v(x) = 3x^2 - 2x\text{ m/s}$. Find its acceleration $a$ at $x = 2\text{ m}$.
questions.explanation: At $x = 2\text{ m}$, $v = 3(4) - 4 = 8\text{ m/s}$ and $\frac{dv}{dx} = 6x - 2 = 10\text{ s}^{-1}$. Thus $a = v\frac{dv}{dx} = 8 \times 10 = 80\text{ m/s}^2$.

questions.prompt: An alternating current is $I(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$. Find its Root-Mean-Square value $I_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\langle I^2 \rangle}$ over one full period $T = 2\pi/\omega$.
questions.explanation: Since $\langle \sin^2(\omega t) \rangle = \frac{1}{2}$ over a full period, $\langle I^2 \rangle = \frac{I_0^2}{2} \implies I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$.
